notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Agriculture is the cultivation of crops and rearing of animals for food, fibre, raw materials and other human needs.
  • It includes:
  • Crop cultivation.
  • Horticulture.
  • Animal husbandry.
  • Dairying.
  • Poultry.
  • Fisheries and allied activities in broader agricultural usage.
  • Agriculture is strongly influenced by climate, soil, water availability and relief.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Agriculture → Crops + Livestock + Allied Activities

2. Importance of Agriculture in India

Agriculture is important because it:

  • Provides food.
  • Supports rural livelihoods.
  • Supplies industrial raw materials.
  • Creates demand for manufactured goods.
  • Supports transport and trade.
  • Provides inputs for exports and agro-processing.
3. Agriculture and India's Geography

India has diverse agricultural systems because of variations in:

  • Rainfall.
  • Temperature.
  • Soil.
  • Relief.
  • Irrigation.
  • Length of growing season.
  • Market access.
4. Agricultural Diversity

India grows:

  • Tropical crops.
  • Subtropical crops.
  • Temperate crops.
  • Food grains.
  • Commercial crops.
  • Plantation crops.
  • Horticultural crops.
5. Factors Affecting Agriculture

Major factors include:

Natural factors:

  • Climate.
  • Soil.
  • Relief.
  • Water.

Human factors:

  • Labour.
  • Technology.
  • Irrigation.
  • Capital.
  • Markets.
  • Transport.
  • Government policy.
6. Relief and Agriculture
  • Plains favour:
  • Mechanisation.
  • Irrigation.
  • Large-scale cultivation.
  • Hills favour:
  • Terrace farming.
  • Plantation crops.
  • Horticulture.
7. Soil and Agriculture

Different soils favour different crops.

Examples:

  • Alluvial → Rice, wheat, sugarcane.
  • Black → Cotton.
  • Red → Millets, groundnut and pulses.
  • Laterite → Tea, coffee, rubber under suitable management.
8. Climate and Agriculture

Agricultural success depends on:

  • Temperature.
  • Rainfall.
  • Humidity.
  • Frost-free period.
  • Sunshine.
9. Rainfall and Agriculture
  • Indian agriculture is strongly influenced by the monsoon.
  • Rainfall affects:
  • Sowing.
  • Soil moisture.
  • Reservoir storage.
  • Groundwater recharge.
  • Crop yield.
10. Monsoon Dependence
  • A large part of Indian agriculture is directly or indirectly dependent on monsoon rainfall.
  • Even irrigated agriculture depends partly on monsoon-fed reservoirs and groundwater recharge.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Indian Agriculture → Monsoon Sensitive

11. Agricultural Seasons

India has three major crop seasons:

  • Kharif.
  • Rabi.
  • Zaid.
📌 Must-Memorise

Crop Seasons → Kharif + Rabi + Zaid

12. Kharif Season
  • Kharif crops are generally sown with the arrival of the southwest monsoon.
  • Sowing usually begins around June-July.
  • Harvesting generally takes place in September-October or later depending on the crop and region.
13. Major Kharif Crops

Important Kharif crops include:

  • Rice.
  • Maize.
  • Bajra.
  • Jowar in many regions.
  • Cotton.
  • Groundnut.
  • Soybean.
  • Tur.
  • Jute.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kharif → Monsoon Crops

14. Rabi Season
  • Rabi crops are generally sown after the southwest monsoon.
  • Sowing commonly occurs during October-December.
  • Harvesting usually occurs during spring.
15. Major Rabi Crops

Important Rabi crops include:

  • Wheat.
  • Barley.
  • Gram.
  • Mustard.
  • Peas.
  • Some pulses.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rabi → Winter Crops

16. Zaid Season
  • Zaid is a short cropping season between Rabi and Kharif.
  • It occurs mainly during summer months.
  • Irrigation is usually important.
17. Major Zaid Crops

Examples include:

  • Watermelon.
  • Muskmelon.
  • Cucumber.
  • Vegetables.
  • Fodder crops.
18. Kharif vs Rabi

Kharif:

  • Monsoon season.
  • Warm and wet.
  • Rice, cotton, groundnut.

Rabi:

  • Winter season.
  • Cool and relatively dry.
  • Wheat, gram, mustard.
19. Food Crops

Food crops are cultivated mainly for human consumption.

Important groups include:

  • Cereals.
  • Millets.
  • Pulses.
20. Commercial Crops

Commercial or cash crops are grown largely for sale and industrial use.

Examples include:

  • Cotton.
  • Jute.
  • Sugarcane.
  • Tobacco.
  • Oilseeds.
  • Plantation crops.
21. Subsistence Farming
  • Subsistence farming produces mainly for the farmer's family.
  • It generally uses:
  • Smaller holdings.
  • Family labour.
  • Limited market orientation.
22. Commercial Farming
  • Commercial farming produces primarily for the market.
  • It generally uses more:
  • Capital.
  • Irrigation.
  • Improved seeds.
  • Machinery.
  • Market inputs.
23. Intensive Farming
  • Intensive farming seeks high output from a relatively small area.
  • It often involves:
  • Multiple cropping.
  • Irrigation.
  • Fertilisers.
  • High labour input.
24. Extensive Farming
  • Extensive farming uses larger land areas with relatively lower input per unit of land.
  • It is less common in densely populated agricultural regions of India.
25. Primitive Subsistence Farming

Traditional forms may involve:

  • Small plots.
  • Simple tools.
  • Family labour.
  • Dependence on natural fertility and rainfall.
26. Shifting Cultivation
  • Shifting cultivation involves clearing a plot, cultivating it temporarily and later moving to another area.
  • It is traditionally practised in some forested hill regions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Shifting Cultivation in Northeast → Jhum

27. Regional Names of Shifting Cultivation

Examples include:

  • Jhum → Northeastern India.
  • Podu → Parts of Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Odisha.
  • Kumari → Parts of Western Ghats.
  • Bewar → Parts of central India.
28. Plantation Agriculture
  • Plantation agriculture is large-scale specialised cultivation of a commercial crop.
  • It usually requires:
  • Capital.
  • Processing.
  • Transport.
  • Labour.
  • Market access.
29. Major Plantation Crops

Important plantation crops include:

  • Tea.
  • Coffee.
  • Rubber.

Other perennial commercial crops may also be grown in plantation systems.

30. Mixed Farming
  • Mixed farming combines crop cultivation with livestock rearing.
  • It provides:
  • Diversified income.
  • Manure.
  • Animal products.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mixed Farming → Crops + Livestock

31. Dry Farming
  • Dry farming is practised in low-rainfall areas without assured irrigation.
  • Moisture-conservation techniques are important.
32. Dry Farming Crops

Typical crops include:

  • Millets.
  • Pulses.
  • Groundnut.
  • Cotton.
  • Oilseeds.
33. Wet Farming
  • Wet farming is practised where rainfall or irrigation is abundant.
  • Rice is the classic crop associated with wet cultivation.
34. Irrigated Farming
  • Irrigated farming depends on artificial water supply.
  • Major sources include:
  • Canals.
  • Wells.
  • Tube wells.
  • Tanks.
  • Reservoirs.
35. Rainfed Farming
  • Rainfed farming depends mainly on rainfall.
  • It is vulnerable to:
  • Delayed monsoon.
  • Long dry spells.
  • Drought.
36. Cropping Pattern
  • Cropping pattern means the proportion of cultivated land devoted to different crops at a given time.
  • It varies across regions.

Detailed crop-pattern geography follows in Chapter 20.

37. Factors Affecting Cropping Pattern

Important factors include:

  • Climate.
  • Soil.
  • Irrigation.
  • Market prices.
  • Food demand.
  • Technology.
  • Government support.
38. Multiple Cropping
  • Multiple cropping means growing more than one crop on the same land during a year.
  • It increases cropping intensity.
39. Cropping Intensity

Cropping intensity is calculated as:

Gross Cropped Area ÷ Net Sown Area × 100

📌 Must-Memorise

Cropping Intensity → GCA/NAS × 100

40. Crop Rotation
  • Crop rotation means growing different crops sequentially on the same field.
  • It can:
  • Maintain soil fertility.
  • Reduce pests.
  • Break disease cycles.
41. Legumes in Crop Rotation
  • Legumes such as pulses can improve soil nitrogen through symbiotic nitrogen fixation.
  • Rhizobium bacteria occur in root nodules.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pulses → Rhizobium → Nitrogen Fixation

42. Intercropping
  • Intercropping means growing two or more crops simultaneously in a planned pattern on the same field.
  • It can improve:
  • Resource use.
  • Risk distribution.
  • Soil cover.
43. Mixed Cropping
  • Mixed cropping involves growing two or more crops together without a definite row arrangement.
  • It reduces risk of total crop failure.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Mixed Cropping ≠ Intercropping

44. Monoculture
  • Monoculture means growing a single crop over a large area or repeatedly.
  • It can simplify farm ecosystems and increase vulnerability to specific pests.
45. Agricultural Holding
  • An agricultural holding is land operated as one farming unit.
  • Holdings may be:
  • Marginal.
  • Small.
  • Semi-medium.
  • Medium.
  • Large.

Exact classification thresholds should be taken from the relevant official agricultural census if asked.

46. Fragmentation of Holdings
  • Fragmentation occurs when farms are divided into small scattered plots.
  • It can reduce efficiency of:
  • Mechanisation.
  • Irrigation.
  • Farm management.
47. Consolidation of Holdings
  • Consolidation combines scattered plots into more compact holdings.
  • It can improve farm efficiency.
48. Agricultural Inputs

Important inputs include:

  • Seeds.
  • Water.
  • Fertilisers.
  • Manure.
  • Pesticides.
  • Machinery.
  • Labour.
  • Credit.
49. Seeds
  • Quality seed strongly influences crop productivity.
  • Improved varieties may provide:
  • Higher yield.
  • Disease resistance.
  • Shorter duration.
  • Stress tolerance.
50. High-Yielding Varieties
  • HYV seeds were an important component of the Green Revolution.
  • They respond strongly to:
  • Irrigation.
  • Fertilisers.
  • Proper crop management.
51. Green Revolution
  • The Green Revolution refers to rapid increases in food-grain production using modern agricultural technology.
  • It expanded especially from the mid-1960s.
  • Wheat showed particularly strong early gains.
📌 Must-Memorise

Green Revolution → Mid-1960s → HYV + Irrigation + Fertilisers

52. Main Components of Green Revolution

Important components included:

  • HYV seeds.
  • Irrigation.
  • Chemical fertilisers.
  • Pesticides.
  • Farm mechanisation.
  • Institutional support.
53. Green Revolution — Initial Core Regions

Early major beneficiaries included:

  • Punjab.
  • Haryana.
  • Western Uttar Pradesh.

Other irrigated regions later adopted similar technologies.

54. Green Revolution and Wheat
  • Wheat responded especially well to HYV technology.
  • Northwestern India became an important centre of high-productivity wheat farming.
55. Green Revolution and Rice
  • High-yielding rice varieties also expanded.
  • Irrigated parts of:
  • Punjab.
  • Haryana.
  • Andhra Pradesh.
  • Tamil Nadu.
  • Other regions benefited.
56. Benefits of Green Revolution

Major benefits included:

  • Higher food-grain production.
  • Improved food availability.
  • Greater use of agricultural technology.
  • Expansion of irrigation.
57. Green Revolution Challenges

Challenges included:

  • Regional inequality.
  • Unequal access to inputs.
  • Groundwater depletion.
  • Soil degradation.
  • Excess fertiliser use.
  • Pesticide pollution.
  • Reduced crop diversity in some areas.
58. Green Revolution and Punjab-Haryana
  • Intensive wheat-rice cultivation increased output.
  • Long-term concerns include:
  • Falling groundwater.
  • Soil stress.
  • Crop-residue burning.
  • Monocropping.
59. Green Revolution in Tamil Nadu
  • Irrigated regions of Tamil Nadu adopted improved rice and other crop varieties.
  • Kaveri delta and irrigated plains benefited from modern inputs.
60. White Revolution
  • White Revolution refers to the rapid expansion of milk production and dairy development.
  • Operation Flood was central to this transformation.
📌 Must-Memorise

White Revolution → Milk

61. Operation Flood
  • Operation Flood was launched in 1970.
  • It helped develop a national dairy network and cooperative model.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Operation Flood → 1970 → Dairy

62. Verghese Kurien
  • Verghese Kurien is widely associated with India's White Revolution.
  • He played a central role in cooperative dairy development.
📌 Must-Memorise

Verghese Kurien → White Revolution

63. Blue Revolution
  • Blue Revolution refers broadly to increased production and development in fisheries and aquaculture.
📌 Must-Memorise

Blue Revolution → Fisheries

64. Yellow Revolution
  • Yellow Revolution is commonly associated with increased oilseed production.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Yellow Revolution → Oilseeds

65. Golden Revolution
  • Golden Revolution is commonly associated with horticulture and increased production of fruits, vegetables and related high-value crops.
66. Horticulture

Horticulture includes cultivation of:

  • Fruits.
  • Vegetables.
  • Flowers.
  • Spices.
  • Plantation crops in broader horticultural classification.
  • Medicinal and aromatic plants.
67. Floriculture
  • Floriculture is cultivation of flowers and ornamental plants.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Floriculture → Flowers

68. Pomology
  • Pomology is the science and cultivation of fruit crops.
📌 Must-Memorise

Pomology → Fruits

69. Olericulture
  • Olericulture is the cultivation of vegetable crops.
📌 Must-Memorise

Olericulture → Vegetables

70. Sericulture
  • Sericulture is the rearing of silkworms for silk production.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sericulture → Silk

71. Apiculture
  • Apiculture is beekeeping.
  • It provides:
  • Honey.
  • Beeswax.
  • Pollination services.
📌 Must-Memorise

Apiculture → Bees

72. Pisciculture
  • Pisciculture is fish farming.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pisciculture → Fish Culture

73. Viticulture
  • Viticulture is cultivation of grapes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Viticulture → Grapes

74. Animal Husbandry
  • Animal husbandry involves breeding and management of livestock.
  • Important animals include:
  • Cattle.
  • Buffaloes.
  • Sheep.
  • Goats.
  • Poultry.
75. Livestock Importance

Livestock provides:

  • Milk.
  • Meat.
  • Eggs.
  • Wool.
  • Manure.
  • Draught power in some areas.
  • Supplementary rural income.
76. Dairying
  • Dairying is the production and marketing of milk and milk products.
  • It provides relatively regular income compared with seasonal crop harvests.
77. Cooperative Dairying
  • Dairy cooperatives aggregate milk from many producers.
  • They facilitate:
  • Collection.
  • Processing.
  • Marketing.
  • Payment to farmers.
78. Poultry Farming
  • Poultry farming involves rearing birds, mainly chickens, for:
  • Eggs.
  • Meat.
79. Sheep Rearing
  • Sheep are important for:
  • Wool.
  • Meat.
  • Dry and semi-arid regions often support pastoral sheep systems.
80. Goat Rearing
  • Goats are adapted to varied climates.
  • They are important for meat, milk and rural livelihoods.
81. Fisheries

Indian fisheries include:

  • Marine fisheries.
  • Inland fisheries.
  • Aquaculture.
82. Marine Fisheries
  • Marine fisheries operate in:
  • Coastal waters.
  • Continental shelf regions.
  • Offshore areas.
  • India's long coastline supports diverse marine fishing.
83. Inland Fisheries

Inland fisheries occur in:

  • Rivers.
  • Lakes.
  • Reservoirs.
  • Ponds.
  • Tanks.
84. Aquaculture
  • Aquaculture is farming of aquatic organisms.
  • It includes:
  • Fish.
  • Shrimp.
  • Shellfish and other organisms.
85. Brackish-Water Aquaculture
  • Brackish-water aquaculture occurs in water with salinity between freshwater and seawater.
  • Coastal shrimp farming is a major example.
86. Agriculture and Irrigation

Irrigation allows:

  • Cultivation during dry periods.
  • Multiple cropping.
  • More reliable yields.
  • Water-intensive crops.
87. Major Irrigation Sources
  • Canals.
  • Wells.
  • Tube wells.
  • Tanks.
  • Reservoirs.
  • Micro-irrigation.
88. Tube-Well Irrigation
  • Tube wells are especially important in alluvial plains.
  • Groundwater can be pumped efficiently where aquifers are productive.
89. Tank Irrigation
  • Tank irrigation is historically important in peninsular India.
  • Tamil Nadu has a major traditional tank network.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Tamil Nadu Traditional Irrigation → Eri/Tank System

90. Drip Irrigation
  • Drip irrigation supplies water near the root zone.
  • It reduces:
  • Evaporation.
  • Runoff.
  • Deep percolation losses.
91. Sprinkler Irrigation
  • Sprinkler systems spray water over crops like artificial rainfall.
  • They are useful on:
  • Uneven land.
  • Sandy soil.
  • Water-scarce farms.
92. Micro-Irrigation
  • Micro-irrigation includes drip and sprinkler systems.
  • It helps increase water-use efficiency.
93. Agricultural Mechanisation

Mechanisation includes use of:

  • Tractors.
  • Harvesters.
  • Seed drills.
  • Pumps.
  • Threshers.
94. Advantages of Mechanisation
  • Faster operations.
  • Reduced dependence on manual labour.
  • Timely sowing and harvesting.
  • Greater efficiency on suitable farms.
95. Limitations of Mechanisation

Challenges include:

  • Small fragmented holdings.
  • High cost.
  • Maintenance requirements.
  • Possible soil compaction from heavy machinery.
96. Fertilisers

Major plant nutrients include:

  • Nitrogen.
  • Phosphorus.
  • Potassium.
📌 Must-Memorise

NPK → Nitrogen + Phosphorus + Potassium

97. Nitrogen

Nitrogen mainly promotes:

  • Vegetative growth.
  • Leaf development.
  • Protein formation.
98. Phosphorus

Phosphorus supports:

  • Root development.
  • Flowering.
  • Energy transfer.
  • Early crop growth.
99. Potassium

Potassium supports:

  • Overall plant vigour.
  • Water regulation.
  • Disease resistance.
  • Stress tolerance.
100. Organic Manure

Examples include:

  • Farmyard manure.
  • Compost.
  • Green manure.
  • Vermicompost.
101. Biofertilisers
  • Biofertilisers contain beneficial microorganisms.
  • They can improve nutrient availability.

Examples include:

  • Rhizobium.
  • Azotobacter.
  • Blue-green algae in suitable systems.
102. Green Manure
  • Green-manure crops are grown and incorporated into soil.
  • They add organic matter and nutrients.
103. Integrated Nutrient Management
  • Integrated nutrient management combines:
  • Organic sources.
  • Chemical fertilisers.
  • Biofertilisers.
  • It aims to sustain soil fertility.
104. Pesticides

Pesticides include:

  • Insecticides.
  • Herbicides.
  • Fungicides.
  • Rodenticides.
105. Insecticide
  • An insecticide controls insect pests.
106. Herbicide
  • A herbicide controls unwanted plants or weeds.
107. Fungicide
  • A fungicide controls fungal diseases.
108. Integrated Pest Management
  • Integrated Pest Management uses a combination of:
  • Biological.
  • Cultural.
  • Mechanical.
  • Chemical methods.
  • It aims to reduce unnecessary pesticide use.
📌 Must-Memorise

IPM → Integrated Pest Management

109. Biological Control
  • Biological control uses natural enemies to control pests.
  • Examples include:
  • Predators.
  • Parasitoids.
  • Pathogens.
110. Weed
  • A weed is an unwanted plant growing where it is not desired.
  • Weeds compete with crops for:
  • Water.
  • Nutrients.
  • Light.
111. Agricultural Productivity
  • Productivity means output per unit of input, often measured as crop yield per hectare.
  • It differs from total production.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Production ≠ Productivity

112. Crop Yield
  • Crop yield is generally expressed as output per unit area.
  • Higher yield does not necessarily mean larger total production if cultivated area is small.
113. Agricultural Production

Total production depends mainly on:

  • Area cultivated.
  • Yield per unit area.
114. Agricultural Diversification
  • Diversification means shifting toward a wider mix of:
  • Crops.
  • Livestock.
  • Horticulture.
  • Fisheries.
  • It can reduce dependence on one crop.
115. Crop Diversification

Benefits include:

  • Risk reduction.
  • Better soil management.
  • Higher-value production.
  • Reduced pressure on water in suitable regions.
116. Sustainable Agriculture

Sustainable agriculture aims to maintain:

  • Productivity.
  • Soil fertility.
  • Water resources.
  • Biodiversity.
  • Farmer livelihoods.
117. Conservation Agriculture

Important principles include:

  • Minimum soil disturbance.
  • Permanent soil cover.
  • Crop diversification.
118. Zero Tillage
  • Zero tillage means sowing crops with minimal or no conventional ploughing.
  • It can:
  • Reduce soil disturbance.
  • Save fuel.
  • Conserve moisture.
119. Mulching
  • Mulching covers the soil surface with crop residues or other materials.
  • It reduces:
  • Evaporation.
  • Erosion.
  • Weed growth.
120. Organic Farming
  • Organic farming avoids or greatly restricts synthetic fertilisers and pesticides.
  • It relies on:
  • Organic manure.
  • Crop rotation.
  • Biological pest control.
  • Ecological nutrient management.
121. Natural Farming
  • Natural farming approaches seek to minimise external synthetic inputs and use locally available biological inputs and ecological processes.
  • Exact programme definitions can vary.
122. Precision Agriculture
  • Precision agriculture uses technology to apply inputs according to local field conditions.
  • Technologies may include:
  • GPS.
  • Sensors.
  • Drones.
  • Satellite data.
123. Protected Cultivation
  • Protected cultivation grows crops under structures such as:
  • Greenhouses.
  • Polyhouses.
  • Shade nets.
  • It allows better environmental control.
124. Greenhouse
  • A greenhouse provides a controlled environment for crop cultivation.
  • Temperature and humidity can be partially managed.
125. Hydroponics
  • Hydroponics grows plants without soil using nutrient solutions.
📌 TNPSC Advanced Fact

Hydroponics → Soil-Less Cultivation

126. Aeroponics
  • Aeroponics grows plants with roots suspended in air and supplied with nutrient mist.
127. Agricultural Drought
  • Agricultural drought occurs when soil moisture is inadequate for crop growth.
  • It can occur even if total seasonal rainfall appears near normal because distribution matters.
128. Meteorological Drought
  • Meteorological drought is significant rainfall deficiency relative to normal.
129. Hydrological Drought
  • Hydrological drought involves reduced:
  • River flow.
  • Reservoir storage.
  • Groundwater.
130. Flood and Agriculture

Floods can:

Benefits:

  • Deposit fresh alluvium.

Damage:

  • Destroy crops.
  • Waterlog fields.
  • Erode soil.
  • Deposit sand over farmland.
131. Cyclones and Agriculture

Cyclones can cause:

  • Crop lodging.
  • Salinity.
  • Flooding.
  • Plantation damage.
  • Livestock losses.

Coastal agriculture is particularly vulnerable.

132. Heat Waves and Crops

High temperature can:

  • Increase evaporation.
  • Reduce flowering.
  • Shorten crop duration.
  • Lower yield.
133. Frost and Agriculture
  • Frost can damage:
  • Vegetables.
  • Fruits.
  • Young crops.
  • Northwestern India and highlands can be affected.
134. Hailstorm Damage
  • Hail can damage:
  • Wheat.
  • Horticultural crops.
  • Vegetables.
  • It may occur with strong thunderstorms and western disturbances.
135. Climate Risk in Agriculture

Important risks include:

  • Drought.
  • Flood.
  • Cyclone.
  • Heat waves.
  • Unseasonal rain.
  • Hail.
  • Pest outbreaks.
136. Climate-Resilient Agriculture

Approaches include:

  • Drought-tolerant crops.
  • Efficient irrigation.
  • Crop diversification.
  • Weather advisories.
  • Soil-moisture conservation.
137. Agro-Climatic Region — Concept
  • An agro-climatic region is an area with similar:
  • Climate.
  • Soil.
  • Water availability.
  • Agricultural potential.
  • Crop planning can be based on these conditions.
138. Agro-Ecological Region
  • Agro-ecological classification also considers:
  • Soil.
  • Landform.
  • Climate.
  • Length of growing period.
139. Length of Growing Period
  • Length of growing period is the period during which temperature and moisture conditions permit crop growth.
  • It is shorter in arid regions and longer in humid regions.
140. Food Security

Food security means that people have reliable access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food.

Agriculture is the physical production base of food security.

141. Agricultural Marketing

Agricultural marketing includes:

  • Assembly.
  • Storage.
  • Transport.
  • Processing.
  • Wholesale.
  • Retail.
142. Storage

Proper storage prevents:

  • Moisture damage.
  • Pest attack.
  • Fungal growth.
  • Post-harvest losses.
143. Cold Storage
  • Cold storage is especially important for:
  • Fruits.
  • Vegetables.
  • Dairy.
  • Fish.
  • Other perishables.
144. Cold Chain
  • A cold chain maintains low temperature during:
  • Storage.
  • Transport.
  • Distribution.
  • It reduces spoilage of perishable products.
145. Warehousing
  • Warehouses store agricultural produce after harvest.
  • They help reduce distress selling and post-harvest losses.
146. Agro-Processing

Agro-processing converts agricultural products into higher-value goods.

Examples:

  • Rice milling.
  • Sugar manufacture.
  • Cotton textiles.
  • Edible oil.
  • Fruit processing.
  • Dairy processing.
147. Agro-Based Industries

Important agro-based industries include:

  • Cotton textile.
  • Jute textile.
  • Sugar.
  • Food processing.
  • Dairy.
  • Vegetable oil.
148. Agricultural Value Chain

The value chain includes:

  • Input supply.
  • Farming.
  • Harvest.
  • Storage.
  • Processing.
  • Transport.
  • Marketing.
149. Post-Harvest Loss

Post-harvest losses can occur because of:

  • Poor storage.
  • Transport damage.
  • Insects.
  • Fungi.
  • Lack of refrigeration.
150. Agricultural Infrastructure

Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected
  • What is agriculture? → Cultivation of crops and rearing of animals and related activities.
  • Main geographical factors controlling agriculture? → Climate, soil, relief and water.
  • Three major crop seasons of India? → Kharif, Rabi and Zaid.
  • When are Kharif crops generally sown? → With the southwest monsoon around June-July.
  • Important Kharif crops? → Rice, maize, cotton, groundnut, soybean and millets.
  • When are Rabi crops generally sown? → During October-December.
  • Important Rabi crops? → Wheat, barley, gram and mustard.
  • What is Zaid? → Short summer cropping season between Rabi and Kharif.
  • Important Zaid crops? → Watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber and vegetables.
  • What is subsistence farming? → Farming mainly for family consumption.
  • What is commercial farming? → Farming mainly for the market.
  • What is intensive farming? → High input and output per unit of land.
  • What is shifting cultivation called in Northeast India? → Jhum.
  • What is Podu? → Regional form of shifting cultivation.
  • What is plantation agriculture? → Large-scale specialised commercial cultivation.
  • Major plantation crops? → Tea, coffee and rubber.
  • What is mixed farming? → Crop cultivation combined with livestock rearing.
  • What is dry farming? → Farming in low-rainfall areas without assured irrigation.
  • What is multiple cropping? → Growing more than one crop on the same land in a year.
  • Formula for cropping intensity? → Gross Cropped Area ÷ Net Sown Area × 100.
  • What is crop rotation? → Growing different crops sequentially on the same field.
  • Why are pulses useful in crop rotation? → Rhizobium helps fix atmospheric nitrogen.
  • What is intercropping? → Growing multiple crops in a planned row arrangement.
  • What is mixed cropping? → Growing multiple crops together without a definite row pattern.
  • What is Green Revolution? → Rapid rise in food-grain production using HYV seeds and modern inputs.
  • When did Green Revolution expand strongly in India? → Mid-1960s onward.
  • Which crop gained strongly in the early Green Revolution? → Wheat.
  • Initial major Green Revolution regions? → Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh.
  • Major Green Revolution inputs? → HYV seeds, irrigation, fertilisers, pesticides and mechanisation.
  • Major environmental problems from intensive Green Revolution farming? → Groundwater depletion, soil stress and chemical pollution.
  • White Revolution relates to? → Milk.
  • Operation Flood launched in? → 1970.
  • Who is associated with White Revolution? → Verghese Kurien.
  • Blue Revolution relates to? → Fisheries.
  • Yellow Revolution relates to? → Oilseeds.
  • What is horticulture? → Cultivation of fruits, vegetables, flowers, spices and related high-value crops.
  • Pomology means? → Fruit cultivation.
  • Olericulture means? → Vegetable cultivation.
  • Floriculture means? → Flower cultivation.
  • Sericulture means? → Silkworm rearing for silk.
  • Apiculture means? → Beekeeping.
  • Pisciculture means? → Fish farming.
  • Viticulture means? → Grape cultivation.
  • What is animal husbandry? → Breeding and management of livestock.
  • What is aquaculture? → Farming of aquatic organisms.
  • Main irrigation sources? → Canals, wells, tube wells, tanks and reservoirs.
  • Traditional Tamil Nadu irrigation system? → Eri/tank system.
  • What is micro-irrigation? → Water-efficient irrigation such as drip and sprinkler.
  • What is drip irrigation? → Supplying water close to plant roots.
  • What is sprinkler irrigation? → Spraying water over crops like rainfall.
  • NPK stands for? → Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
  • Main role of nitrogen? → Vegetative growth.
  • Main role of phosphorus? → Root development and energy transfer.
  • Main role of potassium? → Plant vigour and stress resistance.
  • What is a biofertiliser? → Beneficial microorganism-based input improving nutrient availability.
  • What is IPM? → Integrated Pest Management.
  • What is crop productivity? → Output per unit area.
  • Is production the same as productivity? → No.
  • What is agricultural diversification? → Expansion into varied crops and allied activities.
  • What is conservation agriculture? → Farming based on minimum soil disturbance, soil cover and crop diversification.
  • What is zero tillage? → Crop establishment with little or no conventional ploughing.
  • What is hydroponics? → Growing plants without soil using nutrient solution.
  • What is agricultural drought? → Insufficient soil moisture for crops.
  • What is agricultural extension? → Transfer of scientific farming knowledge to farmers.
  • How does remote sensing help agriculture? → Crop mapping, drought monitoring and crop-health assessment.
  • Why is a cold chain important? → It reduces spoilage of perishable agricultural products.
  • Main agricultural features of Northern Plains? → Fertile alluvium, irrigation and intensive cultivation.
  • Main dryland crops of Deccan regions? → Millets, pulses, cotton, groundnut and oilseeds.
  • Main crop of Kaveri delta? → Paddy.
  • Why is Tamil Nadu agriculture unusual climatically? → Much of it depends strongly on northeast monsoon rainfall.
  • Three important Tamil Nadu paddy seasons? → Kuruvai, Samba and Thaladi.
  • Which paddy season is short-duration and important in Kaveri delta? → Kuruvai.
  • Which Tamil Nadu region is famous for turmeric? → Erode.
  • Which region is famous for tapioca and sago? → Salem.
  • Major Tamil Nadu tea region? → Nilgiris.
  • Madurai is famous for which agricultural product? → Jasmine.
  • Krishnagiri is famous for? → Mango.
  • Theni is known for? → Grapes and banana.
  • Kanyakumari is important for? → Rubber and coconut.
  • Tamiraparani basin supports which important crops? → Paddy and banana.
  • Why are tanks important to Tamil Nadu agriculture? → They store monsoon runoff and support irrigation and groundwater recharge.
